course.title: Linguistics
course.description: How language is built, used, learned and changed: sounds, words, sentences, meaning, use, change, acquisition and variation, ending with a data puzzle in which you work out a language from examples.
course.audience: A capable adult who speaks English well and has never studied linguistics. They know basic grammar words (noun, verb) from school.

paragraphs: Say “cats”, “dogs” and “buses” aloud and listen to the end of each word. The spelling gives all three the same ending, and yet you pronounce three different sounds, /s/, /z/ and a whole extra syllable, and you would choose the right one for a noun you had never heard before. Nobody taught you that rule, and most English speakers couldn't state it, but every one of them follows it. Linguistics is the study of knowledge like this, what you know when you know a language, and it works it out from what speakers actually say and accept.

Because speakers cannot state what they know, linguists study it by treating speech as data. A pair of words that differ in a single sound, a child's “I goed”, or the way Latin pater and English father begin is a small piece of evidence, and with a few careful methods we can turn pieces like these into rules and test the rules on cases they weren't built from. Once you can do that, you can take a handful of words from a language you have never studied, line them up, and say how they are built.
outcomes: You'll be able to describe a consonant by place, manner and voicing.
You'll be able to find phonemes with minimal pairs and state a sound rule.
You'll be able to divide a word into morphemes and a sentence into constituents.
You'll be able to tell an entailment from an implicature.
You'll be able to use regular sound correspondences to relate languages, read a child's error as rule learning, and read an accent or register pattern as social evidence.
You'll be able to work out a pattern from data in an unfamiliar language.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on English: Reading, Writing and Rhetoric.

modules.title: Language and its sounds
modules.description: What a linguist is describing, how speech sounds are made, and how a language organises them into a small set of contrasts.

modules.title: Words and sentences
modules.description: How words are built from parts, how words group into phrases, and how languages differ in how they order them.

modules.title: Meaning and use
modules.description: What a sentence means as a matter of its words and structure, and what a speaker conveys by saying it in a context.

modules.title: Change, learning and society
modules.description: How languages change in regular ways, how children acquire one, how it varies across speakers, and a data puzzle that uses everything.

concepts.title: Descriptive
concepts.summary: Stating what speakers actually say and accept, without ranking it as right or wrong.

concepts.title: Prescriptive
concepts.summary: Stating what speakers ought to say, according to a rule set by an authority.

concepts.title: Arbitrariness
concepts.summary: The link between a word's sound and its meaning is set by convention and not by resemblance.

concepts.title: Place of articulation
concepts.summary: Where in the mouth the airflow is narrowed or blocked: lips (bilabial), teeth and lip (labiodental), tongue ridge (alveolar), soft palate (velar).

concepts.title: Manner of articulation
concepts.summary: How the airflow is shaped: a full stop of air (stop), a narrow channel (fricative) or air through the nose (nasal).

concepts.title: Voicing
concepts.summary: Whether the vocal folds vibrate during the sound.

concepts.title: Phoneme
concepts.summary: A sound that distinguishes words in a language, such as /p/ and /b/ in 'pat' and 'bat'.

concepts.title: Allophone
concepts.summary: One of the different pronunciations of a phoneme that never distinguishes words in the language.

concepts.title: Minimal pair
concepts.summary: Two words that differ in exactly one sound and have different meanings.

concepts.title: Morpheme
concepts.summary: The smallest unit of form that carries meaning or grammatical function.

concepts.title: Inflection
concepts.summary: An ending that marks a grammatical feature such as plural or past without making a new word.

concepts.title: Derivation
concepts.summary: An affix that makes a new word, often changing its category: happy to happiness.

concepts.title: Constituent
concepts.summary: A group of words that works as a single unit in a sentence.

concepts.title: Phrase
concepts.summary: A constituent built around a head word, such as a noun phrase around a noun.

concepts.title: Structural ambiguity
concepts.summary: A sentence with one string of words and two structures, so two meanings.

concepts.title: Basic word order
concepts.summary: The usual order of subject, object and verb in a plain declarative sentence.

concepts.title: Recursion
concepts.summary: A rule that can apply to its own output, so that a phrase can sit inside a phrase of the same kind.

concepts.title: Embedding
concepts.summary: A clause placed inside another clause.

concepts.title: Entailment
concepts.summary: Sentence A entails B if B must be true whenever A is true.

concepts.title: Compositionality
concepts.summary: The meaning of a sentence is built from the meanings of its parts and how they are combined.

concepts.title: Sense and reference
concepts.summary: Reference is the thing a phrase picks out; sense is the way it picks it out.

concepts.title: Implicature
concepts.summary: What a speaker conveys beyond what the sentence entails, by relying on the listener to assume the speaker is cooperative.

concepts.title: Maxim
concepts.summary: One of Grice's four expectations of a cooperative speaker: say enough (Quantity), say what you believe true (Quality), be relevant (Relation), be clear (Manner).

concepts.title: Speech act
concepts.summary: An action done by saying something, such as promising or requesting.

concepts.title: Cognate
concepts.summary: A word in two languages that descends from one word in their common ancestor.

concepts.title: Sound change
concepts.summary: A regular shift in how a sound is pronounced, which affects every word with the sound in the same position.

concepts.title: Language family
concepts.summary: A group of languages descended from one ancestor, such as Indo-European.

concepts.title: Overregularisation
concepts.summary: Applying a rule to a word that is an exception, as in 'goed' or 'mouses'.

concepts.title: Wug test
concepts.summary: A task in which a child is shown a nonsense creature and asked to complete 'two ...', to test whether they apply a rule to a new word.

concepts.title: Milestone
concepts.summary: A typical stage reached at about a given age.

concepts.title: Accent
concepts.summary: A way of pronouncing a language.

concepts.title: Dialect
concepts.summary: A variety of a language with its own vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation.

concepts.title: Sociolinguistic variable
concepts.summary: A feature that speakers realise in different ways depending on who they are and the setting.

concepts.title: Interlinear gloss
concepts.summary: A line of text with morpheme-by-morpheme meanings written beneath it.

concepts.title: Noun class
concepts.summary: A grammatical group of nouns that take the same prefixes, as in Swahili.

concepts.title: Paradigm
concepts.summary: A table of the forms of a word or of a set of words.

lessons.title: What linguists describe

steps.headline: A speaker can tell whether a sentence fits the patterns of the language even when the sentence has no sense.

lead.text: Look back at the first two sentences. Both use the same five words, yet an English speaker accepts one as a possible sentence and rejects the other. The first, “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously”, is the sentence Noam Chomsky wrote in *Syntactic Structures* in 1957, and he chose it because it means nothing at all. Nothing can be colourless and green, ideas don't sleep, and nobody sleeps furiously. Even so, it feels like an English sentence in a way that “Furiously sleep ideas green colorless” does not.

What you are sensing is a difference between **form** and **sense**. A sentence is **well-formed** when its words stand in an order and take endings that the language allows, and it has sense when it describes something that could be so. Chomsky's sentence is well-formed with no sense, and its reversal is neither. The two properties come apart, which tells us something about what a speaker knows: you can recognise a pattern without being able to say anything with it.

afterFigure.text: The third sentence, “The cat sat on the mat”, has both, and every speaker accepts it at once. Notice that none of your three verdicts came from a rule you could quote. You judged by ear, and the first job of a linguist is to take that judgement seriously.

lead.text: The buttons show the three sentences again, and once you answer, each part is labelled by its role.

reveal.text: The reversal fails in form: no English speaker puts an adverb, a verb and then a string of adjectives in that order. Chomsky's sentence fails only in what it describes, and it is the structure that lets us say so.
The linguist is the one reporting what speakers do. The teacher is ranking the sentences, which is a different job, and the next screen gives each job its name.

steps.headline: A descriptive claim says what speakers do, and a prescriptive claim says what they should do.

lead.text: Both people in the last question were making claims about English, but the claims are different in kind. A **descriptive** claim states what speakers actually say and accept, without ranking it, and it can be checked by listening: “speakers of this dialect say ‘I seen it’” is true or false depending on what they do. A **prescriptive** claim states what speakers ought to say, on the authority of a teacher, an editor or a style guide, and it cannot be settled by listening, because a speaker who ignores the rule has not made it false.

Linguists work descriptively, and the reason is not that they think rules are wrong. They are trying to find out what a speaker knows, and what speakers do is the evidence for that. So when you hear that a spoken pattern is “ungrammatical” because a teacher would mark it, the word is doing prescriptive work. For a linguist, a pattern is well-formed if speakers of that variety produce it and accept it.

The same goes for writing. Speech is far older than writing, many languages have never been written, and children learn to speak without lessons, whereas reading has to be taught. It would be odd to call the written form the real language and the spoken form a poor copy of it.

afterFigure.text: A style guide can still be useful. Formal writing has conventions, and knowing them is a skill, but the linguist records a convention as a convention and keeps it separate from the description.

reveal.text: It says nothing about what anyone should do. Someone could test it by counting, and counting could show it to be false, which is the mark of a descriptive claim.

steps.headline: The sound of a word is tied to its meaning only by convention, and that is why a language can be learned and why languages differ.

lead.text: The words dog, chien and Hund name the same animal in English, French and German. If a word's sound were drawn from the animal, they would have something in common, and they have almost nothing. Nothing about the sounds /d/, /ɒ/, /ɡ/ pulls toward a dog. Speakers of English use that sound for the animal because the speakers around them did, and speakers of French do the same with a different sound. We call this property **arbitrariness**: the link between a word's sound and its meaning is set by convention and not by resemblance.

A few words do imitate a sound. English says *cock-a-doodle-doo* for a rooster and French says *cocorico*, and the two are not the same either, because even imitation is filtered through the sounds each language has. So the exception supports the rule. If you meet a word for the first time, nothing in it tells you its meaning, which is why vocabulary has to be learned one word at a time.

afterFigure.text: The point has a consequence for everything else in this course: whatever structure a language has must live in how its sounds and words are arranged, since the words themselves carry no meaning by looks alone.

steps.headline: A grammar lets a speaker produce and understand sentences no one has said before, and that is what a linguist's description has to capture.

lead.text: Here is a sentence you have almost certainly never met before: “The purple walrus recited the tax code to a nervous lighthouse.” You understood it at once, and you could have said it, although nobody taught it to you. A language can't be a list of sentences to remember, because new ones are made all the time. What a speaker has instead is a set of patterns for combining words, and the patterns do the work.

A very small sum shows how much work they do. Give a language 20 nouns and 5 verbs, allow only the pattern noun, verb, noun, and it already has 2,000 sentences. Real languages can also put a sentence inside another one (“she thinks that he knows that…”), so there is no longest sentence. Linguists call this property **productivity**, and a **grammar**, for a linguist, is a description of what a speaker knows that makes it possible.

afterFigure.text: That is the goal of the next eleven lessons, taking a language apart into the parts a speaker is using without noticing: sounds, then words, then sentences, then what they mean.

lessons.orientation: Tell a descriptive claim from a prescriptive one, and judge a sentence by its form apart from its sense.
lessons.nextAction: Describe a consonant by where it is made, how the air is shaped and whether the vocal folds vibrate.

blocks.text: Three strings of words: “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously”, “Furiously sleep ideas green colorless” and “The cat sat on the mat”. Which of them would you accept as English? Most people say the third without thinking, and most also accept the first, although it makes no sense, and reject the second, which uses the very same words as the first in reverse order.

That small judgement is the evidence a linguist works from. Nobody ever told you the rule that separates the first two strings, and yet you apply it at once and in the same way as other English speakers, which means it is something you know without having been taught. Linguistics sets out to describe that knowledge from what speakers actually say and accept, and seeing it that way lets you tell a claim about how people speak from a claim about how they ought to, and a sentence that makes no sense from one that isn't English at all.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether a claim about language describes what speakers do or prescribes what they should do, and to tell a sentence that is odd in meaning from one that is ill-formed.
intro.whyItMatters: Everything else in linguistics rests on this: what speakers do is the evidence, and rules are findings.

recap.keyIdea: Linguists describe what speakers do and accept, a sentence can be well-formed without making sense, and the link between a word's sound and its meaning is arbitrary.

blocks.text: A descriptive claim reports what speakers say and can be checked by listening, while a prescriptive claim says what they should say and rests on an authority. The two come apart, as they do with form and sense: Chomsky's sentence has the form of English with nothing to describe.

Because words are arbitrary, and because speakers make and understand sentences they have never met, a grammar has to describe a set of patterns that fits in a speaker's head, which is where the course goes next, starting with the sounds.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the sounds of speech apart and describes each consonant by where and how it is made.

lessons.title: Making speech sounds

lead.text: We write a sound between slashes, using the symbols of the International Phonetic Alphabet, so that the spelling doesn't get in the way.

reveal.text: One of the two makes the throat buzz. The buzz comes from the vocal folds, which the next screen describes.

steps.headline: A sound is voiced when the vocal folds vibrate while it is made, and voiceless when they do not.

lead.text: Inside your throat are two flaps of tissue called the **vocal folds**. For /z/ they close lightly and the air from the lungs sets them vibrating, which is the buzz you felt. For /s/ they stay apart and the air passes through without making them vibrate. We call a sound that has the vibration **voiced** and a sound without it **voiceless**.

Voicing is about vibration and not about volume. A shouted /s/ is still voiceless and a quiet /z/ is still voiced, and that is why the finger on the throat works at any loudness. Voicing also sorts many other pairs, such as /f/ and /v/, which you can check the same way.

afterFigure.text: Once you can feel the difference, you can use it to find a pair anywhere: the sounds at the start of “sip” and “zip”, “fan” and “van”, “pat” and “bat”.

steps.headline: Place of articulation is where in the mouth the airflow is narrowed or blocked.

lead.text: Now make /p/ and then /t/ and then /k/ and notice where the closure happens. For /p/ your lips meet, for /t/ the tip of your tongue touches the ridge just behind your top teeth, and for /k/ the back of your tongue rises against the soft part of the roof of your mouth. These three sounds are made in three different places, and the place is called the **place of articulation**.

Each place has a name taken from the parts that meet. A sound made with both lips is **bilabial**, one made with the lower lip and the top teeth, such as /f/, is **labiodental**, one made at the ridge behind the top teeth is **alveolar**, and one made at the soft palate, or velum, is **velar**. Use the buttons to see where each of these sits in the mouth.

afterFigure.text: The vocal folds sit below all of these places, which is why voicing can be varied freely while the place stays the same.

reveal.text: The same place can host several sounds: /p/, /b/ and /m/ all close the lips, and what separates them is voicing and the way the air leaves.

steps.headline: Manner of articulation is how the airflow is shaped, and many consonants come in pairs that differ only in voicing.

lead.text: Place says where, and **manner of articulation** says how. For /p/, /t/ and /k/ the airway is closed completely for a moment and then released, and a sound made like that is a **stop**. For /s/ and /f/ the tongue or lip leaves a narrow channel, so the air hisses through, and such a sound is a **fricative**. For /m/ and /n/ the mouth is closed but the soft palate is lowered, so the air flows out through the nose, and these are **nasals**.

Look at the grid with the places as columns and the manners as rows. In many cells there are two sounds, and they differ in voicing alone: /p/ and /b/, /t/ and /d/, /k/ and /ɡ/, /f/ and /v/, /s/ and /z/. The nasals are all voiced, so they stand alone. A name for any consonant now needs three words: voicing, place and manner, in that order, so /z/ is a voiced alveolar fricative.

afterFigure.text: Three features are enough to say which consonant is meant, and that is a good deal fewer than the letters we would need to describe its spelling.

steps.headline: Name the sound /ɡ/, as in “go”, with the three features.

workedSteps.text: Start with voicing. Your throat vibrates when you say “go” slowly, so the sound is voiced.
Next, place. The back of the tongue rises to the soft palate, which is the velum, so the place is velar.
Last, manner. Finish the name by saying how the air is shaped.

reveal.text: Three features pick out one consonant in the grid. The cell in the nasal row and the alveolar column holds one sound only.

steps.headline: Letters and sounds are different things: a word can have more letters than sounds, or fewer.

lead.text: Write “ship” and count four letters, then say it slowly and count three sounds, because the letters s and h together stand for a single sound, /ʃ/. “Knight” has six letters and three sounds, since the k is silent and igh stands for the vowel /aɪ/. “Box” goes the other way: it has three letters and four sounds, since x stands for /k/ followed by /s/ (in a British accent the vowel is /ɒ/, and an American accent uses a different vowel without changing the count).

The letter c shows the same thing from another side, because a single letter can stand for more than one sound. This is why linguists work with sounds written in the IPA and not with spelling: in the IPA each symbol stands for one sound, in every language. Counting sounds means counting the symbols between the slashes.

afterFigure.text: Spelling is a record of the history of the word as much as a guide to its sound, a point the course returns to when it studies how languages change.

lessons.orientation: Describe a consonant by voicing, place and manner, and count the sounds in a word.
lessons.nextAction: Decide which differences between sounds change a word, and state the rule behind the English plural.

blocks.text: The word “ship” has four letters and three sounds, while “box” has three letters and four. Our spelling hides how many sounds a word really has, and it hides something more useful as well: the sounds in a word are made with the lips, the tongue and the throat in ways we can describe exactly.

The description needs only three features for a consonant: whether the throat buzzes while it is made, where in the mouth the air is narrowed or stopped, and how the air gets through. With those three you can name any consonant, in English or in a language you have never heard, and count the sounds in a word without being misled by the way it is spelled.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to describe a consonant by place, manner and voicing, and say how many sounds a word has.
intro.whyItMatters: Three features are enough to name any consonant in the grid, and the same description works for any language.

recap.keyIdea: A consonant is described by its voicing, its place of articulation and its manner, and a word's sounds are counted separately from its letters.

blocks.text: Voicing says whether the vocal folds vibrate, place says where in the mouth the air is blocked or narrowed, and manner says how it is shaped, so /z/ is a voiced alveolar fricative and /p/ is a voiceless bilabial stop.
Because spelling and sound come apart, we count sounds by the IPA symbols between the slashes. “Ship” has three sounds, “knight” has three and “box” has four.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks which of these differences a language uses to separate one word from another.

lessons.title: Contrasts, phonemes and sound rules

steps.headline: A phoneme is a sound that can separate two words, and a minimal pair is the evidence for it.

lead.text: Say “pat” and then “bat”. The two words share a vowel and a final sound, and they differ in the first sound alone, and yet they mean different things. A pair of words that differ in exactly one sound and mean different things is a **minimal pair**, and it tells us that the sounds that differ, here /p/ and /b/, do real work in English. We call a sound that can separate words in this way a **phoneme**.

The test is a practical one. To find out whether two sounds are different phonemes in a language, look for a minimal pair, and if you find one, you know the speakers of that language use the difference to keep words apart. English has minimal pairs for /s/ and /z/ (“sip” and “zip”), for /ʃ/ and /tʃ/ (“ship” and “chip”), and for many more, which is how we know that all of them count.

afterFigure.text: Notice what the test leaves out. It doesn't ask whether two sounds are easy to hear apart, only whether the language uses the difference.

reveal.text: One sound swapped for another, with everything else the same, is what “minimal” means in the name.

lead.text: To most English speakers' ears, the two words contain the same p.

reveal.text: The paper flutters for one of the two. The next screen explains why a difference we can feel need not count as a difference to the language.

steps.headline: Two different pronunciations of one phoneme are allophones when the position of the sound decides which one occurs.

lead.text: In “pin” the /p/ is released with a puff of air, which we call **aspiration** and write [pʰ]. In “spin” the /p/ comes straight after /s/ and has no puff, and we write it [p]. Square brackets mark the sound as actually pronounced, and slashes mark the phoneme. You can hear and feel the difference, and yet English speakers hear one /p/ in both words, because no pair of English words differs only in this.

We call the two pronunciations **allophones** of the phoneme /p/. The choice between them is not free: aspiration appears at the start of a stressed syllable and is absent after /s/, so the position settles it and the difference never separates two words. Another language can treat the same difference differently. In Hindi, for example, aspirated and unaspirated stops are separate phonemes, so a speaker of Hindi would hear the difference that an English speaker ignores.

afterFigure.text: A difference we can hear is not automatically a difference that matters. Whether it matters is a fact about the language, and a minimal pair is how we find out.

steps.headline: The English plural ending has three pronunciations, and the final sound of the noun decides which.

lead.text: Say “cats”, “dogs” and “buses” slowly. The spelling gives each the same ending, s or es, but the sound differs. After “cat” you hear /s/, after “dog” you hear /z/, and after “bus” you hear a whole extra syllable, /ɪz/. Put a finger on your throat for the end of “dogs” and you will feel what lesson 2 called [[voicing|Whether the vocal folds vibrate during a sound. Met in 'Making speech sounds'.]]: the ending vibrates after a voiced sound and doesn't after a voiceless one.

So the rule says that the plural ending is /s/ after a voiceless sound such as /t/, /k/ or /p/, /z/ after a voiced sound such as /ɡ/, /b/ or a vowel, and /ɪz/ after a **sibilant**, which is one of the hissing or hushing sounds /s z ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ/. The extra vowel keeps the two hissing sounds from running together. A speaker doesn't memorise the plural of each noun, and the proof is that the same rule applies to words they have never heard.

afterFigure.text: The spelling hides all of this, because the same letter s is used for /s/ and /z/. The rule is stated in terms of sounds, and so it is only visible once you write the sounds down.

steps.headline: Find the plural ending sound of “cups”, /kʌps/, step by step.

workedSteps.text: Find the last sound of the singular noun. “Cup” is /kʌp/, so the last sound is /p/.
Ask whether /p/ is a sibilant, one of /s z ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ/. It is a stop made with the lips, so it is not, and the ending is not /ɪz/.
Ask whether /p/ is voiced. Your throat does not vibrate for /p/, so it is voiceless.
A voiceless sound takes the voiceless ending. Say which ending that is.

steps.headline: Find the plural ending sound of “bushes”, working from the singular /bʊʃ/.

workedSteps.text: The last sound of “bush” is /ʃ/, the sound of sh.
Ask whether /ʃ/ is a sibilant. It is a hushing sound, so it belongs to the group /s z ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ/.
A sibilant takes the extra vowel before the ending. Write the plural ending sound.

blocks.text: Say “pat” and “bat”. The two words are the same except for the first sound, and that one sound is enough to turn one word into another. Not every difference you can hear does this, though. The p of “pin” and the p of “spin” are pronounced differently, as a strip of paper held at your lips will show, and yet no English speaker treats them as different sounds.

So which differences count is a fact about each language, and a linguist finds it out by looking for pairs of words like “pat” and “bat”. That gives you a way to say which sounds a language keeps apart, and from there to state a sound rule, such as the one that decides how the ending of “cats”, “dogs” and “buses” is pronounced and lets you predict it for a word you have never heard.

recap.keyIdea: A phoneme is a sound that separates words, shown by a minimal pair, and the plural ending's sound depends on the final sound of the noun.

blocks.text: Two sounds are different phonemes of a language when a minimal pair separates them, as /p/ and /b/ are in “pat” and “bat”. Two pronunciations that never separate words, such as [pʰ] in “pin” and [p] in “spin”, are allophones of one phoneme.
The English plural shows a rule at work: the ending is /s/ after a voiceless sound, /z/ after a voiced sound and /ɪz/ after a sibilant, and the same rule covers an invented word like “plog”.

lessons.title: Words are built from parts

reveal.text: The answer shows that a morpheme is not a syllable, and the next screen gives the name for such a piece.

steps.headline: A word is built from morphemes, the smallest parts that carry meaning or a grammatical job.

lead.text: “Cats” breaks into cat, which names an animal, and -s, which means more than one. Neither piece can be cut smaller without losing its meaning, so each is a **morpheme**, the smallest unit of form that carries meaning or grammatical function. Notice that the pieces are not found by counting beats: “unbreakable” has four syllables and three morphemes, un-, break and -able.

A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, like *break* or *cat*, is **free**, and one that has to be attached to something else, like -able or -s, is **bound**. The central piece that carries the core meaning is the **root**, and the bound pieces added to it are **affixes**: a **prefix** goes before the root, as un- does, and a **suffix** goes after it, as -able does. The figure marks each block with its kind and meaning, and the spelling can shift slightly at the join, as when happy becomes happi- before -ness.

afterFigure.text: Finding morphemes is detective work on meaning, since you test each candidate piece by asking whether it contributes something that recurs in other words: un- in “unkind” and “unfair”, -s in “dogs” and “books”.

workedSteps.text: Find the root, the central piece with the core meaning. Here it is happy.
Look before the root for a prefix. The un- at the start means “not”, and it recurs in “unkind” and “unfair”.
Look after the root for a suffix. The -ness turns an adjective into a noun, as in “kindness”.
List the pieces and count them. Say how many morphemes the word has.

steps.headline: Inflectional affixes mark a grammatical feature of a word, and derivational affixes make a new word.

lead.text: Compare the endings in “walked” and “happiness”. The ending -ed puts the verb *walk* into the past, and walked is still the same verb, which is why a dictionary lists walk and not walked. We call an ending that marks a grammatical feature such as plural, past tense or possession, without making a new word, **inflection**. The ending -ness works differently, because it builds the noun *happiness* from the adjective *happy*, a new word with its own entry in the dictionary and a new category. An affix that does this is **derivation**.

A useful test is to ask whether the affix changes the word's category or only its grammatical form. The suffix -s on “cats” stays within the noun category, so it is inflection, as is the -s of “walks” in “she walks”, where it marks the third person singular. Inflection also tends to close a word: you can add -ness to many words and then add -s afterwards, but not the other way round, so “happinesses” is fine and “happysness” is not.

afterFigure.text: One caution: a final s in the spelling does not make a plural. The s in “bus” and “is” belongs to the root.

steps.headline: Languages differ in how much they pack into a word, and Turkish packs a whole phrase into one.

lead.text: The Turkish word evlerimizden is one word with a very long meaning: “from our houses”. It splits into ev, “house”, -ler, the plural, -imiz, “our”, and -den, “from”, so it has four morphemes. English says the same thing with three words, *from*, *our* and *houses*, in which the last carries the plural -s as an affix.

The comparison shows that a **word** is not the unit of meaning. The morpheme is, and different languages tie their morphemes together differently, some into long words like this one, some into short words with many small ones apart. When you meet an unfamiliar language it is a mistake to expect English's habits. The last lesson of the course asks you to find the morphemes of a language you have never seen.

afterFigure.text: Turkish tends to add its endings one after another in a fixed order, which makes its words easy to cut at the joints.

blocks.text: Take the word “unbreakable”. It is a single word, but you understand it by pieces: un- means “not”, break is what it says, and -able means “can be”, and you know that “unbreakable” means can't be broken because you put the three together. Say it aloud, though, and you hear four beats, un-break-a-ble, so the pieces of meaning are not the same as the beats.

A word, then, has a structure of its own, made of pieces that each carry a meaning. Once you can find those pieces, you can work out a word you have never met from parts you already know, tell an ending that makes a new word from one that only marks the plural or the past, and cut up the words of a language you have never studied.

recap.keyIdea: A word is built from morphemes, the smallest parts with meaning, and an affix is inflectional when it marks a grammatical feature and derivational when it makes a new word.

blocks.text: You find morphemes by looking for pieces that recur with the same meaning, which is why “unbreakable” has three and “bus” has one, whatever the number of syllables or letters. An inflectional affix such as -ed leaves the word as the same verb, and a derivational one such as -ness gives a new noun from an adjective.
Languages bundle morphemes differently: Turkish ties four into evlerimizden, where English uses three words.

lessons.title: Words into phrases

reveal.text: Notice that one short word covers a group of three. The next screen asks what that tells us about the sentence.

steps.headline: Words in a sentence form groups, and a group that works as a single unit is a constituent.

lead.text: It is tempting to see a sentence as a line of words in a row, but your reply to the last question shows otherwise. The word *it* took the place of “the small dog”, three words at once, to give “It chased the cat”. In the same way “the cat” can be replaced, to give “The small dog chased it”. A group of words that works as a single unit in this way is a **constituent**, and the test of replacing a group by one word is the **substitution test**.

What the test gives us is a sentence with layers. “The small dog” is a group, “the cat” is another, and “chased the cat” is a larger group that holds one inside it, and a linguist draws these layers as brackets or as a tree with the whole sentence at the top. The tree isn't something we put on the sentence; it records what your replacements already showed. Use the buttons to look at the brackets, the tree and the replacement.

steps.headline: A second test moves the group, and a phrase is a constituent built around a head word.

lead.text: The substitution test has a partner. If a group is a unit, you can usually move it to the front as one piece: “It was the cat that the small dog chased”. We call this the **movement test**. A string that isn't a unit doesn't survive it, as you can hear from “It was chased the that the small dog cat”, because the pieces belong to different groups.

Many constituents are built around one word that sets their category, which we call the **head**. The head of “the cat” is the noun *cat*, so the group is a **noun phrase**, and the head of “chased the cat” is the verb *chased*, so it is a **verb phrase**. A sentence is made of phrases, which are made of smaller phrases and words, and that is what the tree shows.

afterFigure.text: Two independent tests that agree give us far more confidence than one.

reveal.text: A string that doesn't move as a piece is not a unit, however natural the words sound together.

steps.headline: One string of words can have two structures, and each structure gives a different meaning.

lead.text: Consider “I saw the man with the telescope”. It has two meanings: the man has the telescope, or I used a telescope to see him. The words don't change between the two. What changes is where the phrase “with the telescope” attaches. In the first reading it belongs to “the man”, giving the noun phrase “the man with the telescope”, and in the second it belongs to the verb phrase “saw the man”, saying how the seeing was done.

A sentence that has one string and two structures shows **structural ambiguity**. It doesn't depend on any word having two meanings, and that answers the natural guess that two readings must come from two different words. They come from two different groupings, which is why this is the strongest argument that the structure is real: you can't see it in the string, and yet it changes the meaning.

afterFigure.text: You can test each reading with the substitution test: “I saw him” fits the first, since “the man with the telescope” is one unit, and “I saw him with it” fits the second.

Inside “saw the man”, the noun phrase is what I saw. Say which phrase that is.

lessons.orientation: Find constituents with the substitution and movement tests, and see how one string can have two structures.
lessons.nextAction: Name the basic word order of a language and count how deeply a sentence is embedded.

blocks.text: Take the sentence “I saw the man with the telescope” and ask who had the telescope. Some readers say the man did and some say I did, and both are right, although no word in the sentence has two meanings, so the words stay the same while the meaning splits in two.

If the words don't differ, something else must, and it is the way the words are grouped, which the string of words on the page doesn't show. Linguists find the groups with simple tests, such as replacing a group by a single word, and with those tests you can draw the structure of a sentence and show how one string of words can carry two meanings.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find a sentence's constituents with the substitution and movement tests, and show how one string can have two structures.
intro.whyItMatters: Structure is the reason two sentences with the same words can mean different things.

recap.keyIdea: Words in a sentence form groups called constituents, found with the substitution and movement tests, and one string can have two structures with two meanings.

blocks.text: A group of words that can be replaced by one word, or moved as a piece, is a constituent, and the groups are built around head words, so that a noun gives a noun phrase and a verb a verb phrase. A string like “small dog chased” fails both tests, since it cuts across the groups.
Structural ambiguity shows the groups are real: “I saw the man with the telescope” has two structures that differ in where “with the telescope” attaches.

lessons.title: Order, difference and recursion

reveal.text: Many readers guess the English order, because it feels natural, and that's the habit the next screen takes apart.

steps.headline: Languages differ in their basic order of subject, object and verb, and English is only one of several.

lead.text: In a plain statement, a language has a usual order for the subject (S), the verb (V) and the object (O), which we call its **basic word order**. English says “She read the book”, so it is SVO. Japanese says “Tarō ga ringo o tabeta”, Taro, apple, ate, with the verb last, so it is SOV, and the little words *ga* and *o* mark which noun is the subject and which is the object. Irish says “Léigh sé an leabhar”, read he the book, with the verb first, so it is VSO. Six orders are possible in principle, and all six turn up in the atlas.

The English order isn't the natural one, and it isn't even the most common. The World Atlas of Language Structures, a survey of 1,376 languages, finds 564 SOV, 488 SVO, 95 VSO, and the rest spread between rarer orders and languages with no dominant one. A speaker of Japanese doesn't find the English order odd for being unusual, but for being different.

steps.headline: A rule that can apply to its own output lets a clause sit inside a clause, and so lets a sentence grow without any fixed limit.

lead.text: The old nursery rhyme gives a clean example. “This is the cat.” Add a clause to the noun: “This is the cat that chased the rat.” Add another to the new noun: “This is the cat that chased the rat that ate the malt.” Each clause, **that chased the rat** and **that ate the malt**, sits inside the clause before it, and we call a clause placed inside another clause **embedding**.

What makes this possible is a rule that can be applied to its own result: a [[noun phrase|A constituent built around a noun, such as “the cat”. Met in 'Words into phrases'.]] can contain a clause, and that clause can contain a noun phrase, which can contain a clause. A rule that can feed its own output like this is **recursive**, and the property is **recursion**. Notice what the rule says and what it doesn't. It says there is no largest sentence, because one more clause can always be added. It doesn't say speakers produce huge sentences, since they run out of breath and memory long before the rule runs out. The rule is a fact about what they know, and the limit is a fact about what they can do.

blocks.text: “She read the book.” In English the verb sits between the subject and the object, and most English speakers assume that's simply how a sentence goes. Irish puts the verb first, “read he the book”, and other languages make other choices, so the English order turns out to be one option among several, and not even the most common one.

Languages differ in the order of subject, verb and object, and a linguist can count how often each order turns up across the world. What they share runs deeper, since every language can put a clause inside a clause as often as a speaker likes, which is why no language has a longest sentence. With these ideas you can name a language's basic word order and measure how deeply one clause is built into another.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name a language's basic word order and count how many clauses are embedded in a sentence.
intro.whyItMatters: Languages differ a good deal on the surface, and a few properties, such as recursion, appear to be shared.

recap.keyIdea: Languages differ in their basic order of subject, object and verb, and all can embed a clause in a clause because the rule that does it is recursive.

blocks.text: English is SVO, Japanese is SOV and Irish is VSO, and a survey of 1,376 languages finds SOV and SVO the two most common. None of the orders is more natural than the others.

A recursive rule lets a clause contain a clause of the same kind, so the number of clauses has no upper limit in principle, though speakers can only manage so many. We count the embedded clauses and leave out the main one.

lessons.title: What a sentence entails

reveal.text: You don't need any more facts to answer. That's the idea of entailment, and the next screen gives it a test.

steps.headline: Sentence A entails sentence B when B must be true whenever A is true, and a test finds it.

lead.text: The sentence “Mira killed the spider” has a consequence: the spider died. We say that the first sentence **entails** the second, because the second must be true whenever the first is. The test is to suppose the first sentence true and try to make the second false, and if you can't, the entailment holds. For “killed” you can't, since a spider that was killed is dead.

Now try “Mira swatted the spider”. This sentence makes the death likely, but you can imagine it true while the spider scuttles away, so the test fails and there is no entailment. People often count anything they would infer as an entailment, and the test is stricter than that: it asks whether the reverse is *possible*, and not whether it is likely. A third kind of entailment comes from word meanings: “It is a poodle” entails “It is a dog”, because every poodle is a dog. The figure draws each case as a ring of situations.

afterFigure.text: The entailment runs one way only, and the third case shows it: a dog doesn't have to be a poodle.

steps.headline: A sentence's meaning is built from the meanings of its parts and how they are combined, and two forms can give the same truth conditions.

lead.text: We can say what a sentence means by saying in which situations it would be true, which are its **truth conditions**. “The dog bit the postman” is true when a dog sank its teeth into a postman. The meaning is built up from the words and their structure, a principle we call **compositionality**, and it explains why swapping the nouns gives a different sentence: “The postman bit the dog” has the same words in another structure and a different set of situations.

Now compare “The postman was bitten by the dog”. The structure has changed and the order of the nouns is reversed, but the dog is still the biter, so the two sentences are true in exactly the same situations. They differ in emphasis, in which noun phrase begins the sentence, and not in what they say about the world. A speaker who thinks they differ in meaning is hearing the change in emphasis.

afterFigure.text: Truth conditions give us a way to compare any two sentences: ask whether any scene can make one true and the other false.

lead.text: Use the figure to switch the sentence between active, passive and a form with no agent at all.

reveal.text: Look at who is doing the biting in each of the first two versions. The third leaves the biter out and changes what we are told.
The specific term entails the general one in each of the true cases, and a general term can't entail a specific one.

steps.headline: Test whether “Sam sold the old car to Lee” entails “Sam sold a car”.

workedSteps.text: Suppose the first sentence is true, so Sam sold an old car to Lee.
Try to make the second false: Sam must not have sold any car at all.
That clashes with the first sentence, because the old car is a car and Sam sold it. No situation makes A true and B false.
State the verdict as a yes or no.

steps.headline: Now reverse the test: does “Sam sold a car” entail “Sam sold the old car to Lee”?

workedSteps.text: Suppose the first is true, so Sam sold some car to someone.
Look for a situation in which the second is false while the first stays true. Sam could have sold a new car, or sold it to Ana.
A single such situation breaks the entailment. State the verdict.

steps.headline: A phrase's reference is the thing it picks out, and its sense is the way it picks it out.

lead.text: In 1892 the German philosopher Gottlob Frege published a paper, *Über Sinn und Bedeutung*, in which he pointed out a puzzle. The morning star and the evening star are the same planet, Venus. If a phrase meant only the thing it named, “the morning star is the evening star” would say no more than “the morning star is the morning star”. Yet the first sentence was a discovery, and the second is empty.

Frege's answer was to separate two things. The **reference** of a phrase is the thing it picks out, which here is Venus for both. The **sense** is the way it picks the thing out, which here is *seen before sunrise* for one and *seen after sunset* for the other. Two phrases can share a reference and differ in sense, and a sentence that equates them can be informative for that reason. So “same reference” doesn't mean “same meaning”.

afterFigure.text: Sense is why we can be surprised by an identity, and reference is why we can say that a sentence is true or false about the world.

blocks.text: Take the sentence “Mira killed the spider” and suppose it is true. Some further facts come with it whatever else happened in the scene, while others are only likely, so that you would expect them and could still imagine them failing. Compare it with “Mira swatted the spider”, which describes much the same scene with a different verb, and ask whether the two sentences tell you the same things about the spider.

Linguists call a consequence that has to come with a sentence an **entailment**, and it gives us a way to compare the meanings of sentences without asking anyone what they feel they mean, because we only have to ask which situations would make each one true. With it you can test whether one sentence follows from another, and say why two phrases that pick out the same thing can still differ in meaning.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to test whether one sentence entails another, and say how a phrase's sense differs from its reference.
intro.whyItMatters: Entailment gives meaning a test that anyone can run.

recap.keyIdea: A sentence entails another when no situation makes the first true and the second false, and a phrase's sense is a different thing from its reference.

blocks.text: You test an entailment by supposing the first sentence true and looking for a situation in which the second is false: “killed” entails “died” and “poodle” entails “dog”, while “swatted” doesn't entail “died”. Active and passive sentences are true in the same situations, so they differ in emphasis only.
Frege showed that two phrases can have the same reference and different senses, which is why “the morning star is the evening star” can be news.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from what a sentence means to what a speaker means by saying it, which can be a good deal more.

lessons.title: What a speaker conveys

reveal.text: Most listeners conclude more than the sentence entails, and the rest of this lesson asks where the extra part comes from.

steps.headline: What a sentence entails and what a speaker implicates are different, and the cancel test tells them apart.

lead.text: The sentence “Some of the students passed” [[entails|A entails B when B must be true whenever A is true. Met in 'What a sentence entails'.]] that at least one student passed, since it can't be true otherwise. It doesn't entail that *not all* passed, and yet that is what we usually understand. We call something a speaker conveys beyond what the sentence entails an **implicature**, and the test that separates it from an entailment is the **cancel test**: add a phrase that denies the consequence, and see whether the result is a contradiction.

Add “but none did” and you get a contradiction, so *at least one passed* is part of what is said, and cannot be cancelled. Add “in fact, all of them did” and the sentence is perfectly fine, so *not all passed* was never entailed. A hearer who concluded it was reading it from the situation. The figure sets the two attempts side by side.

afterFigure.text: An entailment can't be cancelled, and an implicature can, and the difference shows where the meaning comes from.

diagram.alt: A sentence, Some of the students passed, followed by an attempt to cancel one of its consequences. Cancelling at least one passed with but none did gives a contradiction. Cancelling not all passed with in fact all of them did gives no contradiction.

steps.headline: Hearers assume that speakers are cooperating, and four expectations explain what they read into a sentence.

lead.text: Why do we conclude *not all* from “some”? The philosopher H. P. Grice argued, in lectures he developed in the 1960s and published in 1975 as “Logic and Conversation”, that conversation is a cooperative effort, and that hearers expect speakers to follow four **maxims**. **Quantity**: say as much as is needed, and no more. **Quality**: say what you believe to be true. **Relation**: be relevant. **Manner**: be clear and orderly.

Now run the argument for “some”. If every student had passed, a cooperative speaker would have said “all”, because “all” is more informative and Quantity asks for enough. The speaker said “some”, so the hearer concludes that “all” wasn't available, which is to say not all passed. That reasoning is not about the word *some*. It is about what a cooperative speaker would have said otherwise, which is why the conclusion can be cancelled when the speaker adds that all did.

afterFigure.text: Notice that no one is lying. The speaker said something true, and the hearer drew a conclusion from the assumption of cooperation.

Hearers usually take it to mean exactly three. A speaker with four would be expected to say so, by Quantity.
Run the cancel test on the stronger reading by adding “in fact, she has four”.

steps.headline: Saying something can be doing something, and some words take their meaning from the context of the speaker.

lead.text: Speakers don't only describe the world. The philosopher J. L. Austin, whose lectures at Harvard in 1955 were published in 1962 as *How to Do Things with Words*, pointed out that to say “I promise to call” is to make a promise, and that “Can you pass the salt?” at dinner is a request in the form of a question. An action done by saying something is a **speech act**, and the same words can perform different acts in different contexts.

A related point is that some words can't be understood without the situation of the speaker. “I”, “here” and “now” are cases: they refer to whoever speaks, wherever they are, whenever they speak. Words like these are called **deictic**, and they show that the meaning of a sentence is only part of what is conveyed when someone says it.

afterFigure.text: We are about to see that this is what makes the study of use a separate subject from the study of meaning.

reveal.text: The literal reading would be a question about ability, and nobody takes it that way. Hearers read the act from the situation, using the same assumption of cooperation.

blocks.text: “Some of the students passed.” Read strictly, the sentence says that at least one student passed, and it would stay true if every student had passed. What a listener takes from it in an ordinary conversation can be more than that, and the extra part comes from somewhere other than the words.

The philosopher H. P. Grice traced it to an assumption every hearer makes about a speaker, namely that the speaker is cooperating in the conversation. Once you can see that assumption at work, you can separate what a sentence entails from what a speaker only suggests, using a test that needs one added phrase, and say which of the hearer's expectations is doing the work.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell an entailment from an implicature with the cancel test, and name the maxim that explains it.
intro.whyItMatters: Meaning in use includes what we infer about the speaker, which a theory of sentences alone can't capture.

recap.keyIdea: An entailment can't be cancelled and an implicature can, and implicatures arise because hearers assume speakers follow Grice's maxims.

blocks.text: “Some of the students passed” entails that at least one passed, and it implicates that not all did, because a cooperative speaker who knew all had passed would have said so. Adding “in fact, all of them did” cancels the implicature and leaves the sentence consistent.
Speech acts add that saying things is doing things, as with “Can you pass the salt?”, and deictic words like “I” and “here” depend on the situation of the speaker.

lessons.title: How languages change

reveal.text: The same match in pair after pair is too regular to be an accident, and the next screen says what produces it.

steps.headline: Cognates are words that descend from one word in an ancestor language, and they differ by regular sound correspondences.

lead.text: The pairs have the same meaning and the same shape, and each Latin /p/ meets an English /f/. Latin tres and English three begin with /t/ and /θ/, and canis and hound begin with /k/ and /h/. Words like these are **cognates**, words in two languages that descend from a single word in their common ancestor. Latin did not turn into English, and neither borrowed from the other. Both go back to a language spoken thousands of years ago that we call Proto-Indo-European, and each has changed it in its own way.

The mark of cognates is that the differences are not random. Wherever Latin has /p/ at the start of a word, English has /f/, and the same goes for /t/ and /θ/ and for /k/ and /h/. We call a match like this a **sound correspondence**. In 1786 Sir William Jones, a judge in Calcutta, told the Asiatic Society that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were so alike that they must have come from a common source, and the regularity of the matches is what later made that claim testable. The pattern in the figure is named Grimm's law, after Jacob Grimm.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows three matches. Each one is a rule about a sound, and not about a word.

steps.headline: Sound change is regular, which is how inherited words are told from borrowed ones, and change is not decay.

lead.text: A sound change affects *every* word with the sound in the same position, and it doesn't pick words at random. When the Germanic languages changed /p/ to /f/, every inherited word with a word-initial /p/ changed, and no one decided it. That is why the matches in the figure keep recurring. It also gives a test for the other possibility, borrowing: English *father* is inherited, and has /f/, but English *paternal* has the /p/ of Latin, because it was borrowed from Latin long after the change had happened. Likewise *foot* is inherited and *pedal* borrowed, and *heart* is inherited and *cardiac* borrowed from Greek.

Change of this kind isn't corruption. English has changed a great deal since the days of Old English, and no one would say that the change made it worse, since every stage of every language did its work for the people who used it. Seeing a change as a rule that applied to a whole language is better than seeing a word go wrong.

afterFigure.text: A word that breaks the pattern is usually one that arrived by another route, which makes the exceptions informative.

steps.headline: English itself has changed in stages, and four dated events mark them.

lead.text: The same patient comparison works inside one language, because English from a thousand years ago would be hard for you to read. Four dates help to place its stages. In 1066 the Normans conquered England, and the French of the new ruling class brought a great many words into English over the next centuries, beginning the shift from Old English to Middle English. In 1476 William Caxton set up a printing press at Westminster, and printing began to fix spelling and spread one written form. In 1623 Shakespeare's plays were collected in the First Folio, a document of Early Modern English. In 1755 Samuel Johnson published his *Dictionary of the English Language*, which did much to settle the spelling we use now.

None of these events changed the language by decree. Each marks a moment when the language was changing in step with its speakers, and the stages shade into one another, which is why the figure marks the boundaries as approximate.

afterFigure.text: Placing events in order is a first step to seeing which changes belong to which period.

blocks.text: The Latin word for “father” is pater, and the Latin for “foot” is pes. English has father and foot, and the Latin word for “fish” is piscis. In each pair a Latin /p/ meets an English /f/, which would be odd if the words had nothing to do with each other.

Could that be chance? The same match turns up in dozens of pairs, and so do matches between /t/ and /θ/ and between /k/ and /h/, so whatever explains them has to explain all of them at once. Finding that explanation is what lets you tell which words in two languages are related, and even predict a word in one language from its partner in the other.

intro.whyItMatters: Regular sound change turns a list of resemblances into evidence that languages are related.

recap.keyIdea: Cognates descend from one word in a common ancestor and differ by regular sound correspondences, so a correspondence can predict a form and tell inherited words from borrowed ones.

blocks.text: Latin /p/, /t/ and /k/ meet English /f/, /θ/ and /h/ in cognates such as pater and father, tres and three, and canis and hound. Because a sound change affects every word with the sound in the same place, a word like paternal that keeps the old /p/ must have been borrowed.
English has also changed in stages that dates such as 1066, 1476, 1623 and 1755 help to place, and none of the changes was decay.

lessons.title: How children acquire language

reveal.text: The child hadn't heard that form, which makes it more interesting than it looks, as the next screen shows.

steps.headline: A child's overregularisation is evidence that the child has learned a rule and not merely collected forms.

lead.text: Children's errors are rarely random. A child who says “goed” or “mouses” or “foots” is adding the regular ending, -ed for the past and -s for the plural, to a word that is an exception, and we call this **overregularisation**. Adults say *went* and *mice*, so the child hasn't copied these forms. The child has worked out a rule from the regular words, and used it where it doesn't apply.

Notice the order of events. Many children first say “went”, then “goed”, and then “went” again. At the first stage they repeat the adult form without any rule behind it. At the second the rule arrives and spreads to the exceptions, and at the third the child has the rule and the exceptions together. The dip in the curve is a sign of progress, a pattern we call **U-shaped learning**. Even at the low point, children say “went” a good deal of the time, so the curve is a schematic.

afterFigure.text: A language isn't a list of forms to be memorised. The child is doing what the linguist did in the third lesson, working out the rule.

steps.headline: Berko's wug test showed that children apply rules to words they have never heard.

lead.text: How can we be sure that a child has a rule, and isn't just remembering words? In 1958 Jean Berko devised a test that does away with memory. She showed children a picture of a made-up creature and said “This is a wug”, then showed two of them and said “Now there is another one. There are two ___.” No child had ever heard the word *wug*, so no child could have remembered its plural, and yet children completed the sentence with the plural ending a speaker of English would expect.

The ending they used was the one the [[plural rule|The ending is /s/ after a voiceless sound, /z/ after a voiced one and /ɪz/ after a sibilant. Met in 'Contrasts, phonemes and sound rules'.]] picks: the sound of the plural depends on the last sound of the noun, and the children chose accordingly. We call a task of this kind a **wug test**. The same logic applies with other nonsense words, since the child has to apply the voicing rule to a word that no adult has ever given them.

steps.headline: Children reach stages in a typical order, at ages that vary from child to child.

lead.text: Children don't start with sentences. At about six months they begin **babbling**, strings of syllables such as “ba-ba-ba”, which are made of the sounds of speech and have no words in them yet. At about twelve months most produce their first words, and at about eighteen to twenty-four months they begin to combine two words, as in “more milk” or “daddy go”. These ages are **milestones**, the typical points at which a stage is reached.

Two cautions go with them. The ages are approximate, since healthy children differ by months, so a child who reaches a stage a little earlier or later isn't remarkable. And what lies behind the order is still argued about: how much of language is built into children, and how much they learn from what they hear. The wug test and “goed” both show that learning goes beyond the input, since no one provides the plural of *wug*, and the debate is over how much the learner brings to the task.

blocks.text: A two-year-old says “I goed to the shop”, and a few months later says “I went to the shop”. It is natural to hear the first sentence as a slip and the second as the child getting it right, but the first is the more interesting of the two, once you ask where the word *goed* could have come from.

Read that way, a child's mistake becomes evidence of what the child knows, and a linguist can go further by inventing words and seeing what children do with them. With that approach you can read an error as the sign of a rule the child has found, and see the first milestones of speech, from babbling to two-word phrases, as stages that come in a steady order.

lessons.title: Variation and society

reveal.text: It isn't fixed, which is what lets a linguist treat such a feature as a measurement, and the next screens give the vocabulary for it.

steps.headline: Speakers vary in accent, dialect and register, and each is a different kind of difference.

lead.text: Not everyone speaks one way, and linguists have four terms for the ways they differ. An **accent** is a way of pronouncing a language, so two people with different accents can use the same words and grammar. A **dialect** is a variety with its own vocabulary and grammar as well as its own pronunciation, and “lorry” for “truck”, or “I seen it”, belong to dialect. A **register** is the variety a speaker uses for a situation, such as a formal one at a job interview or a relaxed one at home.

A single speaker has more than one register, and sometimes moves between two varieties, or two languages, within one conversation. We call that **code-switching**. None of these is a mistake in a standard. A standard variety is the one that happens to carry social prestige, usually because of who speaks it, and it works no better as a language than the others do.

steps.headline: Labov showed that a pronunciation could mark social class by measuring it in three department stores.

lead.text: In November 1962 the sociolinguist William Labov asked how one could measure a social fact about speech. He chose three New York department stores that were ranked by status: Saks Fifth Avenue, which was highest, Macy's, in the middle, and S. Klein, the lowest. He approached an employee as a customer and asked where something was on the fourth floor, expecting the answer “Fourth floor”. Then he said “Excuse me?”, and got a second, more careful repetition. He noted whether the r after a vowel was pronounced in *fourth* and *floor*.

A feature that speakers realise in different ways depending on who they are and the setting is a **sociolinguistic variable**, and the r here was one. The result was a clear pattern: 62 percent of Saks employees, 51 percent of Macy's and 20 percent of Klein's pronounced the r all or some of the time, and the ranking by r matched the ranking by status. The pattern in the careful repetition was similar, with more r's pronounced than in the first, casual answer. Nobody was told what to look for, and the pattern showed up anyway.

steps.headline: The social pattern shows why a standard variety is socially favoured and not better in itself.

lead.text: Labov's result is a fact about *who* uses which variant of the r, and that fact says nothing about which pronunciation is better. In New York in 1962 the pronounced r carried prestige, and that is why the higher-ranked store had more of it. Nothing about the sound makes it clearer or more correct, and in other places and times the r-less pronunciation has carried the prestige instead. Social status attaches to a variant because of the people who use it, and then speakers adjust, often without noticing, to sound like those they admire.

This is the descriptive attitude from the first lesson applied to society. A linguist doesn't say the r-less speaker is wrong. The linguist says that in this community, in 1962, pronouncing the r signalled status, and that speakers of every group shifted towards it when they spoke carefully.

afterFigure.text: A standard variety is a social fact, not a linguistic virtue.

reveal.text: Labov counted who dropped the r and when. Judging the speakers is something else.
The variation here follows the setting and not the speaker's origin, which is what separates it from a dialect.

blocks.text: Suppose you wanted to measure a social fact about speech, say whether the way someone pronounces a sound tells you something about their position in society. You can't ask people, because they don't know they do it, and listening to one speaker tells you about that speaker and no one else. What would you do?

In 1962 William Labov found a way, in three New York department stores, by getting shop assistants who didn't know they were being studied to say “fourth floor” and listening for the r. Studies built like his let you read a detail of pronunciation as evidence about a community, and tell an accent from a dialect or a register when you hear one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell accent from dialect and register, and read a sociolinguistic variable as evidence of a social pattern.
intro.whyItMatters: Variation is where language and society meet, and it is the field's best evidence that no variety is a mistake.

recap.keyIdea: Accent, dialect and register are different kinds of variation, and a sociolinguistic variable such as the r in “fourth floor” can show a social pattern.

blocks.text: An accent differs in pronunciation, a dialect in words and grammar as well, and a register in the situation the speaker is in. In Labov's 1962 study 62 percent of Saks employees, 51 percent of Macy's and 20 percent of Klein's pronounced the r all or some of the time, in the same order as the stores' status.
The standard variety is the one that is socially favoured, and the result shows how status attaches to a sound without the sound itself being better.

lessons.title: Working out a language from data

reveal.text: The change is small and local. That is what lets you find the parts of a word without knowing the language.

steps.headline: To work out an unknown language, line the forms up, cut each into parts, and match each part to a meaning.

lead.text: Take the three forms nimesoma, umesoma and amesoma. They translate as “I have read”, “you have read” and “s/he has read”, and they share everything but the beginning, so the beginning must carry the difference between *I*, *you* and *s/he*. Next compare nimesoma and nitasoma, which are the same except in the middle, where me and ta swap, and the translation changes from *have read* to *will read*. So the middle must carry the tense. What stays constant in all of them, soma, must mean *read*, and tulipika has a different stem, pika, which suggests *cook*.

We write the result as an **interlinear gloss**, a line of text with the meaning of each part written beneath it: ni-me-soma is *I-perfect-read*. The method is the one from the lesson on [[morphemes|The smallest units of form that carry meaning or grammatical function. Met in 'Words are built from parts'.]]: find the smallest pieces that recur with a constant meaning. The thing to resist is looking for the rule in the translations. The English *have read* is two words, and the Swahili part for it is a single piece, so the translation can't tell you where the cuts go. Only the forms can.

reveal.text: A part that changes when only the tense of the translation changes must be the part that marks the tense.

steps.headline: Work out what tu- means from tulipika, “we cooked”.

workedSteps.text: List what you already know. The past marker -li- appears in walisoma, “they read”.
The stem -pika appears only in this form, and the translation has the verb cook, so -pika is cook.
Cut away the parts you have explained: tu- li- pika. Only tu- is left.
Say which meaning is left over for tu-, from the translation.

steps.headline: Build “they cooked” from the parts you have.

workedSteps.text: The subject for they is wa-, which appears in walisoma.
The past marker is -li-, from walisoma and tulipika.
The stem for cook is -pika, from tulipika. Put the three pieces together in order.

steps.headline: Write the rules as a pattern, test it on every form you have, and then use it to build new forms.

lead.text: Your rules say that a verb has a subject prefix, a tense marker and a verb stem, in that order. Before trusting them, test them on every given form, and not only the ones you used to find them. The test is what separates a pattern from a guess: nimesoma is ni + me + soma, umesoma is u + me + soma, nitasoma is ni + ta + soma, and walisoma and tulipika fit as well. Every form is accounted for, so the pattern passes, and the pieces can be recombined.

That recombination is the point. A **paradigm** is a table of the forms of a word, and with the pattern you can fill in the cells that the data didn't give you, such as *they have cooked*, or *you will cook*. This is what it means to know a language's morphology as a rule, and not as a list, and it is what a child does in the wug test.

afterFigure.text: A pattern that survives a test on a form it wasn't built from is far more convincing than one that merely fits the first few.

steps.headline: Swahili groups its nouns into classes that take the same prefixes, and the verbs agree with them.

lead.text: Nouns have a pattern too. Swahili mtoto, “child”, has the plural watoto, “children”, and mtu, “person”, has watu, “people”, so m- at the start changes to wa-. In another group, kitabu, “book”, has the plural vitabu. A grammatical group of nouns that take the same prefixes is a **noun class**. Swahili is a Bantu language, and noun classes of this kind are a feature of that group.

The classes reach into the verb: the wa- of walisoma, “they read”, is the same wa- as in watoto, and a plural of people takes the same prefix on its verb as a plural of nouns takes on itself. We say the verb *agrees* with its subject. English has a little of this, in *is* and *are*, but Swahili agreement runs through the whole sentence, which is a reminder that languages package their grammar in different ways.

blocks.text: Here are six Swahili verbs and what they mean: nimesoma, “I have read”, umesoma, “you have read”, amesoma, “s/he has read”, nitasoma, “I will read”, walisoma, “they read”, and tulipika, “we cooked”. You haven't studied Swahili, and yet from these six forms you can say “we have cooked” correctly, and you can do it without looking anything up.

You can do it because the language builds each of these words from parts, and the parts can be found by lining the forms up and seeing what changes when the meaning changes. Linguists use exactly this method on a language they are meeting for the first time, and with it you can cut an unfamiliar word into pieces, say what each piece means, and build forms that were never in the data.
