intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out a pattern from data in an unfamiliar language, and use it to build forms you were never given.
intro.whyItMatters: Everything in this course comes together when you face a language you don't know.

recap.keyIdea: A pattern in an unfamiliar language is found by lining forms up, cutting them into parts, matching each part to a meaning and testing the pattern on every form.

blocks.text: From six Swahili verbs you found a subject prefix, a tense marker and a verb stem, and you used them to build forms you had not been given: tumepika, utasoma, walipika. The same method found the noun pattern in mtoto and watoto, and kitabu and vitabu, where a prefix changes in the plural.
What you have done is what the whole course has been about: describing what a speaker knows, from what speakers say, and checking it against every case.

questions.prompt: Chomsky's sentence “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” is faulty in only one way. Is the fault in its form or in its meaning?
hints: An English speaker accepts the word order and the endings. Ask what the sentence fails to describe.
questions.onCorrect: The sentence follows English patterns for subject, verb and adverb, so its form is fine; the trouble is that nothing could be both colourless and green.

misconceptions.feedback: The words are in an order an English speaker accepts, with adjectives before the noun and an adverb after the verb. Compare it with the reversed version, which does fail in form.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Meaning: the form is fine, but nothing can be colourless and green.

questions.prompt: A teacher marks “Whom did you see?” as right and “Who did you see?” as wrong. A linguist writes down that people say both. Which of them is reporting what speakers actually do?
hints: One of them is ranking the sentences. The other is recording them.
questions.onCorrect: A report of what people say can be checked by listening to them, which is why linguists begin there.

misconceptions.feedback: The teacher is ranking the two sentences as right and wrong, which tells us what the teacher thinks people should say.
The teacher's marking ranks the two sentences as right and wrong, which is a judgement about usage and not a report of it.
Writing down what people actually say is a report of usage, and that is what happens in one of the two cases.

questions.prompt: “In everyday speech, English speakers use who far more often than whom.” Is this claim descriptive or prescriptive?
hints: Could you check it by listening to people, or does it tell them what to do?
questions.onCorrect: A descriptive claim can be tested against what speakers do, so it could turn out to be false; a prescriptive claim cannot be tested that way.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the claim tells anyone what to say. It reports how often people use each word, so it can be checked by counting.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Descriptive: it reports how often speakers use each word.

questions.prompt: Nothing about the sound of “dog” ties it to the animal, which is why French uses chien and German uses Hund. What do linguists call this property of words?
hints: The word names a link that is set by convention. The three languages chose differently.
questions.onCorrect: Because the link is arbitrary, speakers of different languages can use unrelated sounds for the same thing.

misconceptions.feedback: A word that imitates a sound would be the opposite case. Here the three sounds share nothing with a dog, so the link comes from convention.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Arbitrariness: the link between sound and meaning is a convention.

questions.prompt: Suppose a second tiny language has 12 nouns and 4 verbs, and every sentence is a noun, then a verb, then a noun. How many different sentences can it make?
hints: Choose the first noun, then the verb, then the second noun.
The number of choices at each slot multiplies.
questions.onCorrect: Each slot multiplies the count, and a real language that lets a sentence contain another sentence has no largest sentence at all.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers of words. The choices combine, so each of the 20 first nouns can go with every verb and every second noun.
That leaves out one of the nouns. The sentence has two noun slots, both with 20 choices.

questions.prompt: A style guide says: “Use fewer with things you can count and less with things you can't.” Is this claim descriptive or prescriptive?
hints: Does the guide report what people say, or tell them what to say?
questions.onCorrect: A guide like this can be useful for formal writing, and it is still a rule set by an authority, so a linguist would record it as a prescription and then check it against usage.

misconceptions.feedback: The guide does not report how people talk. It tells writers which word to choose, which makes it a rule set by an authority.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Prescriptive: it says what writers ought to do.

questions.prompt: “Speakers of this dialect say ‘I seen it’ in casual speech.” Is this claim descriptive or prescriptive?
hints: Does the claim say what speakers do, or what they ought to do?
questions.onCorrect: The claim reports a pattern that can be checked by listening, and it takes no side on whether the pattern is good.

misconceptions.feedback: The claim does not tell anyone what to say. It reports what speakers of the dialect do, so it is descriptive.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Descriptive: it states what speakers of the dialect say.

questions.prompt: Which of these is well-formed but meaningless?
hints: Two of the four follow English patterns. Of those two, only one describes something that could happen.
questions.onCorrect: A speaker can accept the form of a sentence while finding nothing for it to describe.

misconceptions.feedback: This one is well-formed and sensible, so it is neither of the two faults.
This is the first sentence in reverse. It breaks English word order, so it fails in form rather than only in meaning.
This breaks English word order and is not a sentence an English speaker accepts, so its fault is in form.

choices.label: The cat sat on the mat

questions.prompt: “You should never end a sentence with a preposition.” Is this claim descriptive or prescriptive?
hints: The word “should” points to a rule. Who sets it?
questions.onCorrect: English speakers end sentences with prepositions all the time, so a descriptive record would say the pattern is common.

misconceptions.feedback: A description would say what speakers do. This claim says what they should do, and in fact speakers often end sentences with prepositions.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Prescriptive: it says what speakers should do.

questions.prompt: Put a finger on your throat and make a long /s/ and then a long /z/. Which of the two makes your throat vibrate?
hints: Hold each sound for a few seconds and feel the difference.
questions.onCorrect: The vocal folds vibrate for /z/ and stay still for /s/, which is the only difference between the two sounds.

misconceptions.feedback: The hiss of /s/ is made in the mouth, by air rushing past the tongue, and the throat stays still while you make it.
The two sounds feel alike in the mouth, since the tongue is in the same place for both, but under your finger only one of them buzzes.
One of the two does buzz under your finger, and that buzz is the whole difference between them.

questions.prompt: The sound /m/ is made by closing the lips. What is its place of articulation?
hints: The name has two parts, one meaning two and the other meaning lip.
questions.onCorrect: Bilabial combines bi-, two, with labial, of the lips, so /p/, /b/ and /m/ share this place.

misconceptions.feedback: For /m/ the closure is made by the two lips together, without the teeth or the tongue.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bilabial: both lips make the closure.

questions.prompt: Look at the six stops /p b t d k ɡ/. Which of them are voiced?
hints: The six stops make three pairs, one at each place.
The two stops in a pair differ in voicing alone.
questions.onCorrect: Each of the three places has one voiced stop, /b/, /d/ and /ɡ/, and one voiceless stop, /p/, /t/ and /k/.

misconceptions.feedback: For /p/, /t/ and /k/ the vocal folds stay apart, so these are the voiceless member of each pair.
/p/ and /b/ are the two stops made with the lips, and they differ in voicing, so only /b/ of the two is voiced.
Each of the three places has a voiceless stop as well as a voiced one, and the voiceless ones leave the throat still.

questions.prompt: Finish naming /ɡ/ as in “go”: a voiced velar what?
hints: Does the air get through in /ɡ/, or is it blocked completely for a moment?
questions.onCorrect: For /ɡ/ the back of the tongue shuts the airway completely, then lets the air go in a small burst, which is why it is a stop.

misconceptions.feedback: A fricative keeps a narrow channel open so the air hisses through. For /ɡ/ the airway is closed completely first.
A nasal lets air out through the nose. For /ɡ/ the air has no way out until the tongue lets go.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stop: the airflow is blocked completely and then released.

questions.prompt: Which consonant is the voiced alveolar nasal, the sound at the start of “no”? Write the letter you would put between slashes.
hints: Voiced, tongue at the ridge, air through the nose.
questions.onCorrect: A nasal is voiced almost without exception, so /n/ has no voiceless partner in the grid, as /m/ has none either.

misconceptions.feedback: /m/ is also voiced and nasal, but it is made with the lips. The question asks for the tongue ridge.
/d/ and /t/ are made at the same place, but the air stops in the mouth. In the sound asked for the air goes out through the nose.

questions.prompt: How many sounds are in the word “thumb”, which is written /θʌm/? (The letters th stand for one sound.)
hints: Count the symbols between the slashes, not the letters of the spelling.
The th at the start is one sound, and the b at the end is silent.
/θ/, /ʌ/ and /m/.
questions.onCorrect: Spelling and sound come apart: thumb has five letters but only the three sounds /θ/, /ʌ/ and /m/.

misconceptions.feedback: Five is the number of letters. The th is one sound and the b is silent.
Four counts th as two sounds. Between the slashes there are three symbols.

questions.prompt: The letter c is pronounced differently in “cat” and in “city”. Which sounds does it stand for?
hints: Find a word that starts with the same sound as each, such as “kit” or “sit”.
questions.onCorrect: The letter c stands for /k/ in cat and /s/ in city, so a single letter can stand for more than one sound.

misconceptions.feedback: “Cat” does begin with /k/, but “city” begins with the same sound as “sit”, which is /s/.
“City” does begin with /s/, but “cat” begins with the same sound as “kit”, which is /k/.
Say the two words slowly: “cat” starts like “kit” and “city” starts like “sit”, so the sounds are the other way round.

questions.prompt: The sounds /s/ and /z/ differ in one feature only. Which: place, manner or voicing?
hints: Both are made with the tongue at the ridge, with a narrow channel for the air.
questions.onCorrect: Both are alveolar fricatives, and the vocal folds vibrate only for /z/.

misconceptions.feedback: Both sounds are made with the tongue at the ridge behind the teeth.
Both let the air hiss through a narrow channel.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Voicing: /s/ is voiceless and /z/ is voiced.

questions.prompt: What is the place of articulation of /k/?
hints: It is made with the back of the tongue.
questions.onCorrect: The back of the tongue touches the soft palate, or velum, which gives velar its name.

misconceptions.feedback: Alveolar sounds such as /t/ use the tongue tip at the ridge. For /k/ the back of the tongue is raised.
Bilabial sounds such as /p/ use both lips. For /k/ the closure is far back in the mouth.

questions.prompt: How many sounds are in the word “knight”, which is written /naɪt/?
hints: Count the symbols between the slashes.
The two characters in /aɪ/ are the symbol for one sound, a vowel.
The k is silent, so the sounds are /n/, then the vowel, then /t/.
questions.onCorrect: The spelling has six letters, but the sounds are /n/, /aɪ/ and /t/.

misconceptions.feedback: Six is the number of letters. The k is silent and igh stands for a single sound.
The symbol /aɪ/ names a single vowel sound that glides from one position to another.

questions.prompt: The words “pat” and “bat” are /pæt/ and /bæt/. How many sounds do the two words have in common?
hints: Write the sounds of each word in a column and compare them place by place.
The vowels match.
The vowel /æ/ and the final sound /t/ are shared.
questions.onCorrect: Two of the three sounds match, and the one that differs is enough to give each word its own meaning, which makes pat and bat a minimal pair.

misconceptions.feedback: Three is the total number of sounds in each word, and one of them differs: /p/ against /b/.
Compare all three places in the two words. The vowel and the last sound are the same.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: /æ/ and /t/ match, so 2 sounds are shared.

questions.prompt: Which of these pairs of English words is a minimal pair?
hints: A minimal pair differs in exactly one sound, in the same position in both words, and nothing else.
questions.onCorrect: The two words differ only in /f/ and /v/, so English uses that difference to keep words apart, and /f/ and /v/ are separate phonemes.

misconceptions.feedback: “Spin” has an extra sound at the start, so the two words differ in length, and no sound in one stands in the place of a sound in the other.
“Bat” and “tab” have the same three sounds in a different order, so no single sound has been swapped.
“Cats” adds a sound to the end of “cat”, so the words differ in length and not in one sound at the same position.

questions.prompt: Hold a strip of paper close to your lips and say “pin” and then “spin”. For which of the two does the paper move more?
hints: Say each word a few times with the paper in the same place.
questions.onCorrect: The /p/ at the start of “pin” is aspirated, which means it is released with a puff of air, and the /p/ after the s in “spin” is not.

misconceptions.feedback: When a p comes straight after /s/, it is released without a puff, so the paper barely moves.
The two p's sound alike to most English ears, but one of them is released with a puff of air that moves the paper and the other is not.

choices.label: Both move it the same amount

questions.prompt: In English, does the difference between [pʰ] in “pin” and [p] in “spin” separate one word from another? Answer yes or no.
hints: Is there any pair of English words that differ only in aspiration?
questions.onCorrect: English speakers hear both as /p/ because the choice between them is fixed by position. It never decides which word is meant.

misconceptions.feedback: We can hear the difference, but it never separates two English words, since the puff is decided by where the sound falls.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No: the two are allophones of /p/.

questions.prompt: What is the plural ending sound in “cabs”: /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/? The singular is /kæb/.
hints: Is the last sound of “cab” voiced?
questions.onCorrect: The /b/ at the end of cab is voiced, so the plural ending is voiced too, even though it is spelled with an s.

misconceptions.feedback: The spelling suggests /s/, but it follows a voiced sound. Say “cabs” with a finger on the throat and the ending vibrates.
The extra vowel is only needed after a hissing sound, and /b/ is not one.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: what is the plural ending sound in “cups”?
hints: The last sound of “cup” is /p/. Is it voiced?
questions.onCorrect: The final /p/ is voiceless and is not a hissing sound, so the ending is /s/.

misconceptions.feedback: /p/ is voiceless, so the ending cannot vibrate the vocal folds.
The extra vowel comes only after a hissing sound, which /p/ is not.

questions.prompt: What is the plural ending sound in “bushes”? The singular is /bʊʃ/.
hints: Look at the last sound: /ʃ/ is a hushing sound like /s/ and /z/.
questions.onCorrect: After a hissing sound the plural needs an extra vowel, so “bushes” has a separate syllable.

misconceptions.feedback: A plain /s/ would run into the /ʃ/ at the end of the word. A hissing sound needs a vowel between.
A bare /z/ would run into the final /ʃ/. A hissing sound needs an extra vowel.

questions.prompt: A new word, “plog”, /plɒɡ/, names an invented gadget. What plural ending sound would an English speaker use?
hints: Check the last sound of “plog”.
questions.onCorrect: Speakers apply the rule to a word they have never heard, which is how we know it is a rule and not a memorised list.

misconceptions.feedback: The spelling invites /s/, but the final /ɡ/ is voiced and the ending follows it.
The extra vowel follows hissing sounds only. /ɡ/ is not one of them.

questions.prompt: What is the plural ending sound in “dogs”: /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/?
hints: Look at the last sound of “dog”, and say whether it is voiced.
questions.onCorrect: The final sound of dog is voiced, so the ending is voiced as well, although it is written s.

misconceptions.feedback: We spell the ending with s, but the ending follows the voiced /ɡ/ and takes on its voicing.
The extra vowel appears only after hissing sounds.

questions.prompt: What is the plural ending sound in “books”?
hints: Is the last sound of “book” voiced?
questions.onCorrect: The final /k/ is voiceless, so the plural ending is voiceless too.

misconceptions.feedback: /k/ is voiceless. A voiced ending would have to follow a voiced sound.
An extra vowel is added only after a hissing sound, which /k/ is not.

questions.prompt: Which pair is a minimal pair?
hints: A minimal pair has the same number of sounds, and exactly one of them differs.
questions.onCorrect: Sip and zip are identical except for the voicing of the first sound, so /s/ and /z/ are separate phonemes.

misconceptions.feedback: Bat and bed differ in two places, the vowel and the last sound, so they are not a minimal pair.
Pin and spin have different numbers of sounds, and the p in each is the same phoneme.
Cat and catch differ by a whole extra sound at the end, so they differ in more than one place.

questions.prompt: The word “cats” has one syllable. How many pieces of it carry a meaning of their own?
hints: Compare “cat” and “cats”, and ask what the ending adds.
questions.onCorrect: Syllables count beats of sound and morphemes count meaningful parts, so a one-syllable word can have two morphemes.

misconceptions.feedback: A syllable is a unit of sound, and one syllable can hold more than one piece of meaning: the -s adds “more than one” to cat.
The letters c, a and t mean nothing one at a time. Together they name the animal, and the -s adds “more than one”.

acceptedIdeas: Two: cat, and an -s that means more than one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two: cat, and an -s that means more than one

choices.label: One, since it is a single syllable
Two: cat, and an -s that means more than one

questions.prompt: Can the ending -able in “readable” stand alone as a word of English? Is it a free or a bound morpheme?
hints: Try using -able by itself in a sentence.
questions.onCorrect: A bound morpheme must be attached to something. Prefixes and suffixes are bound, and a root that can stand alone is free.

misconceptions.feedback: A free morpheme can be a word by itself, like “read”. The ending -able never appears on its own.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bound: it only occurs attached to another morpheme.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: how many morphemes are in “unhappiness”?
hints: Find the root first, then the pieces before and after it.
The root is happy, with a prefix and a suffix.
un-, happy and -ness.
questions.onCorrect: The root happy has a prefix un- and a suffix -ness, so the word has three morphemes, and it needs four syllables to say.

misconceptions.feedback: Four is the number of syllables, un-hap-pi-ness. Count the meaningful parts instead.
There is a prefix as well as a suffix around the root.

questions.prompt: How many morphemes are in “rewriting”?
hints: Look for a prefix, a root and an ending.
The re- adds the meaning “again”.
re-, write and -ing.
questions.onCorrect: The root write has a prefix re- meaning again and an ending -ing, so there are three morphemes although the spelling drops the final e.

misconceptions.feedback: There is a prefix and an ending around the root.
Five would count letters or syllables. The meaningful parts are re-, write and -ing.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: is -ed in “walked” inflectional or derivational?
hints: Does -ed make a new word with a new meaning, or mark a grammatical feature of the same verb?
questions.onCorrect: -ed marks past tense on the same verb, so walk and walked are forms of one word, which is what inflection means.

misconceptions.feedback: Derivation makes a new word, such as happiness from happy. Walked is the same verb in a different tense.

questions.prompt: The word “bus” ends in the letter s. How many morphemes does it have?
hints: Does “bu” mean anything of its own?
There is no part that means more than one.
The s belongs to the root.
questions.onCorrect: The s in “bus” is part of the root, so the word is a single morpheme, and an ending that looks like a plural need not be one.

misconceptions.feedback: If “bus” were bu + s, bu would have to mean something. It does not, so the s is part of the root.

questions.prompt: Turkish ev means “house” and -imiz means “our”. The word evimizden means “from our house”. How many morphemes does it have?
hints: There is no plural in this word.
Use the pieces you have just met: house, our and from.
ev, -imiz and -den.
questions.onCorrect: The plural -ler of the earlier word is missing, so the word has three morphemes: ev, -imiz and -den.

misconceptions.feedback: Four would include the plural -ler. This word means a single house.
It is one word, but it carries three meaningful parts.

questions.prompt: How many morphemes are in “unbreakable”?
hints: Look for a prefix, a root and a suffix.
The root is break.
un-, break and -able.
questions.onCorrect: The word has a prefix, a root and a suffix, although we say it in four syllables.

misconceptions.feedback: Four counts the syllables un-break-a-ble, not the meaningful parts.
Both the prefix and the suffix carry meaning.

questions.prompt: How many morphemes are in “internationalization”, which is inter + nation + al + ize + ation?
hints: The question has already split the word into pieces.
Count the pieces separated by plus signs.
inter, nation, al, ize, ation.
questions.onCorrect: A long word can pile up several affixes on one root, and each piece adds something to the meaning.

misconceptions.feedback: It is one word, but the pieces show five meaningful parts.
Count the pieces between the plus signs and not the syllables.

questions.prompt: “Internationalization” divides into inter + nation + al + ize + ation. Which of these pieces is its root?
hints: The root carries the core meaning and is often a free morpheme.
questions.onCorrect: Nation is the only piece that can stand alone as a word, and every affix is built around it, one layer at a time.

misconceptions.feedback: Inter- is a prefix meaning “between”, and it can't stand alone as a word, so it can't be the core the other pieces attach to.
-ize is a suffix that turns an adjective into a verb, so it needs something before it to attach to.
-ation is a suffix that turns a verb into a noun, and it is the last piece added, not the core of the word.

questions.prompt: In “happiness”, is the ending -ness inflectional or derivational?
hints: Does -ness make a new word with a different category?
questions.onCorrect: Happy is an adjective and happiness is a noun, so -ness builds a new word with a new category, which is derivation.

misconceptions.feedback: Inflection marks a grammatical feature of the same word, such as past tense. -ness changes an adjective into a noun.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Derivational: it makes a noun from an adjective.

questions.prompt: Take “The small dog chased the cat”. Which single word could replace the words “the small dog” and still leave a sentence?
hints: Try each word in place of “the small dog” and read the sentence aloud.
questions.onCorrect: A pronoun stands in for a whole group of words at once, which suggests that the group works as a single unit.

misconceptions.feedback: “Small chased the cat” has no one doing the chasing, because small only describes the dog.
“Chased chased the cat” repeats the verb and leaves no one to do the chasing.
One short word can stand in for the whole group of three and leave a complete sentence, as a pronoun does.

choices.label: None, since three words can't be replaced by one

questions.prompt: In “The small dog chased the cat”, is “the small dog” the subject or the object?
hints: Who does the chasing?
questions.onCorrect: The whole group fills the subject role, so the unit that plays a role in the sentence is the group and not any single word of it.

misconceptions.feedback: The object is the one affected by the verb, which here is the cat. The dog does the chasing.

questions.prompt: Can “small dog chased” be replaced by a single word, giving a sentence that still works? Answer yes or no.
hints: Try putting it in the place of the group: “The ___ the cat”.
questions.onCorrect: No single word can stand for it, because it takes the end of one group and the start of another, so it is not a constituent.

misconceptions.feedback: Try it: “The ___ the cat” leaves no word that works. The string cuts across the groups.

questions.prompt: A group can be moved into the frame “It was ___ that …”, as in “It was the cat that the small dog chased”. From “The small dog chased the cat”, which of these strings can be moved this way to make a good sentence: “the cat”, “chased the”, “the small dog”?
hints: Put each string into the frame and read the result aloud.
questions.onCorrect: The two real groups can be moved, and “chased the” cannot, because it takes the end of one group and the start of another.

misconceptions.feedback: “It was the small dog that chased the cat” works as well, so the subject passes the test too.
“It was chased the that the small dog cat” falls apart, because chased and the belong to different groups.
“Chased the” takes the verb from one group and the article from another, so it is the one string that can't move as a unit.

acceptedIdeas: “The cat” and “the small dog”, but not “chased the”
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “The cat” and “the small dog”, but not “chased the”

choices.label: “The cat” and “the small dog”, but not “chased the”

questions.prompt: Finish the working: what is a constituent built around a noun, such as “the book”, called?
hints: The group is named after its head word.
questions.onCorrect: A phrase takes its name from its head, the word that gives it its category, so the phrase headed by a noun is a noun phrase.

misconceptions.feedback: A verb phrase is built around a verb, such as “read the book”. “The book” has a noun as its head.

questions.prompt: In the reading where I used the telescope, the object of “saw” is only part of the long phrase. Is it “the man” or “the man with the telescope”?
hints: Which phrase is what I saw, leaving out how I saw it?
questions.onCorrect: In that structure “with the telescope” hangs off the verb phrase and says how I saw, while “the man” is what I saw.

misconceptions.feedback: /t/ would follow a voiceless sound, but /b/ is voiced.
The extra vowel appears after /t/ or /d/, which are not the last sound of “zib”.

questions.prompt: Milestone ages say when a typical child reaches a stage. Are they exact or approximate?
hints: Do all children reach each stage in the same month?
questions.onCorrect: Children vary, so a milestone age is a typical value and a child who reaches a stage a few months earlier or later is not remarkable.

misconceptions.feedback: Children differ, so a milestone age is a typical value around which individual children vary.

questions.prompt: A child says “mouses”. This shows the child:
hints: The child has made a plural, but not the adult one.
questions.onCorrect: The child has the -s plural rule and applies it to a noun that is an exception.

misconceptions.feedback: The child has formed a plural by adding the regular ending, which shows the opposite.
Adults say “mice”, so there is no adult form to copy.
Overregularisation is typical of normal development.

acceptedIdeas: Has learned the plural rule and overapplies it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Has learned the plural rule and overapplies it

choices.label: Has learned the plural rule and overapplies it

questions.prompt: What is the sound at the end of the plural “wugs”: /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/?
hints: Is the last sound of “wug” voiced?
questions.onCorrect: The /ɡ/ in wug is voiced, so the plural ending is voiced too, as in dogs.

misconceptions.feedback: The spelling suggests /s/, but the sound before the ending is voiced, so the ending is voiced as well.
The extra vowel follows hissing sounds only.

questions.prompt: A child is shown a cartoon creature, told its name, and asked to complete “There are two ___”. What is this test called, after the made-up name?
hints: It is named for the creature in the first picture.
questions.onCorrect: Berko's test shows that children apply a rule to a word they have not heard, which imitation alone cannot explain.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are other creatures in the same study. The test took its popular name from the first creature in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Think of a speaker who says “floor” with the r sounded in one setting. What about the same speaker in another setting?
hints: Think of how your own speech changes between a job interview and a chat with friends.
questions.onCorrect: Speakers move between pronunciations depending on the setting, which is why a feature can be a variable and not a fixed property of a person.

misconceptions.feedback: Speakers shift their pronunciation with the setting, speaking more carefully in some situations than in others, so one person can sound the r at one moment and drop it at another.
A speaker who sounds the r in one setting may well sound it in others too; what changes from setting to setting is how often.

acceptedIdeas: They might leave the r out, depending on the setting
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They might leave the r out, depending on the setting

choices.label: They might leave the r out, depending on the setting
They will always sound the r, since a pronunciation is fixed for each person
They will always leave the r out in any other setting

questions.prompt: Two speakers use the same words and the same grammar but pronounce them differently. What is the difference called: accent, dialect or register?
hints: Which of the three names a difference in pronunciation only?
questions.onCorrect: An accent is a way of pronouncing the language, and a dialect adds its own words and grammar to the pronunciation.

misconceptions.feedback: A dialect differs in vocabulary and grammar as well. Here the words and grammar are the same.
Register depends on the situation, such as a formal or casual one, and not on which speaker it is.

questions.prompt: One speaker says “lorry” where another says “truck”. A difference in vocabulary goes beyond accent. What is the variety called?
hints: It involves words, and perhaps grammar, as well as sound.
questions.onCorrect: A dialect has its own vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation, and a speaker of one is not making mistakes in another.

misconceptions.feedback: An accent is a difference in pronunciation only. A different word is more than that.

questions.prompt: In the chart, 62% of Saks employees and 20% of Klein's employees pronounced r all or some of the time. How many percentage points higher is Saks than Klein's?
hints: Subtract the lower percentage from the higher one.
62 minus 20.
Work out the tens first.
questions.onCorrect: The gap is 42 percentage points, which is the size of the difference between the highest and lowest ranked stores.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two percentages. The question asks for the gap.
That is the gap between Saks and Macy's. The question names Klein's.

questions.prompt: In Labov's study, how did the share of employees who pronounced the r compare across the three stores?
hints: Read the three bars in order of the stores' status.
questions.onCorrect: The ranking by r matched the ranking by status, 62, 51 and 20 percent, which is what made the r a social signal.

misconceptions.feedback: The shares were 62, 51 and 20 percent, so they differed a great deal from store to store.
Klein's had the smallest share of the three, 20 percent, against 62 percent at the top-ranked store.
Macy's, at 51 percent, came between the other two, below the top-ranked store at 62 percent.

acceptedIdeas: It was highest at Saks, the top-ranked store, and lowest at Klein's
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It was highest at Saks, the top-ranked store, and lowest at Klein's

choices.label: It was about the same in all three
It was highest at Klein's, the lowest-ranked store
It was highest at Macy's, in the middle
It was highest at Saks, the top-ranked store, and lowest at Klein's

questions.prompt: Finish the working: Macy's scored 51% and Klein's 20%. How many percentage points higher is Macy's than Klein's?
hints: Subtract the lower percentage from the higher one.
51 minus 20.
Work out the tens first.
questions.onCorrect: The gap between the middle and the lowest ranked store is 31 points, larger than the 11 between the top two.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two percentages. The question asks for the gap.
That is the gap between Saks and Macy's.

questions.prompt: “People who drop their r's speak badly.” Is this claim descriptive or prescriptive?
hints: Does it report a pattern, or judge one?
questions.onCorrect: The claim ranks a way of speaking as bad, which is a judgement about status and not a description of a pattern.

misconceptions.feedback: A descriptive claim would report who drops the r and when. This one ranks the speakers.

questions.prompt: A speaker uses formal vocabulary at a job interview and casual words with friends at home. What is this variation by situation called?
hints: The speaker is the same. What changes is the setting.
questions.onCorrect: Register is the variety a speaker chooses to suit a situation, and every speaker has more than one.

misconceptions.feedback: A dialect belongs to a community of speakers. This is one speaker adjusting to a situation.
The difference here is in words and style as well as pronunciation.

questions.prompt: A difference in pronunciation only is called:
hints: Which kind of variation involves sound and nothing else?
questions.onCorrect: An accent is a way of pronouncing a language, with the same vocabulary and grammar.

misconceptions.feedback: A dialect also differs in vocabulary and grammar.
A register depends on the situation and can involve words and grammar as well as sound.
A language is a larger notion, and pronunciation alone doesn't make a different one.

questions.prompt: What sound did Labov count in “fourth floor”?
hints: It occurs after a vowel, in two places in the phrase.
questions.onCorrect: Labov counted whether the r after a vowel was pronounced, in the middle of “fourth” and at the end of “floor”.

misconceptions.feedback: The th was also noted, but the variable that gave the main result was another sound.

questions.prompt: Which store was ranked highest in Labov's study?
hints: Think of the store on Fifth Avenue.
questions.onCorrect: Saks ranked highest, and it also had the highest share of employees who pronounced the r.

misconceptions.feedback: Macy's was the middle-ranked store.
S. Klein was the lowest-ranked of the three.
The study depended on the three stores having clearly different status.

questions.prompt: Compare nimesoma, “I have read”, with nitasoma, “I will read”. How many letters in the first word change to give the second?
hints: Write the two words one above the other and look for the letters that differ.
Both begin with ni and end with soma.
What is left in the middle?
questions.onCorrect: Only the middle changes, me to ta, so that part must carry the difference between have read and will read.

misconceptions.feedback: Six is the length of the shorter pieces together. Compare the two words letter by letter and count the differences.
Both letters of the middle part change, me to ta.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: me becomes ta, which is 2 letters.

questions.prompt: Compare nimesoma, “I have read”, with nitasoma, “I will read”. Where in the word does the difference lie?
hints: Write the two words one above the other and mark the letters that differ.
questions.onCorrect: Only the middle changes, me to ta, so that part must carry the difference between have read and will read.

misconceptions.feedback: Both words begin with ni, which fits the I they share in translation.
Both words end in soma, which fits the read they share in translation.
Most of the two words is identical, with the same start and the same ending, and only two letters differ.

questions.prompt: Compare nimesoma, “I have read”, with nitasoma, “I will read”. What does the middle part -ta- mark: perfect, future or past?
hints: Which English word in the translation corresponds to the part that changed?
questions.onCorrect: The marker -ta- replaces -me- when the translation changes from have read to will read, so it marks the future.

misconceptions.feedback: The perfect is the first word, nimesoma, where the marker is -me-. The second form is the one that has -ta-.
The past appears in walisoma and tulipika, with a different marker.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: tulipika means “we cooked”. The -li- means past and -pika means cook. What does tu- mean?
hints: Remove the parts you already know and see what is left.
questions.onCorrect: Once the past marker and the verb are accounted for, the prefix tu- is left to carry the meaning we.

misconceptions.feedback: They is wa-, which you can see in walisoma. The prefix here is tu-.
I is ni-, in nimesoma and nitasoma.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: how do you say “they cooked”?
hints: Take the subject for they, the marker for the past and the stem for cook.
questions.onCorrect: The form is built from wa- for they, -li- for the past and -pika for cook, so the new word needs no new part.

misconceptions.feedback: That is “we cooked”. The subject for they is wa-.
That is “they read”. The stem for cook is -pika.

questions.prompt: Use the pieces: how do you say “s/he has cooked”?
hints: Subject for s/he, marker for the perfect, stem for cook.
questions.onCorrect: The form is a- for s/he, -me- for the perfect and -pika for cook, assembled in that order.

misconceptions.feedback: That is “s/he has read”. The stem for cook is -pika.
The prefix tu- means we. The subject for s/he is a-.

questions.prompt: In kitabu, “book”, the plural is vitabu, “books”. What replaces ki- in the plural?
hints: Compare the two words and ignore the part they share.
questions.onCorrect: The part that changes is the prefix, ki- to vi-, and the rest of the word stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Wa- replaces m- in mtoto and mtu. In this pair the singular begins with ki-.

questions.prompt: The children have read. Use the patterns: how do you say “they have read”, which fits with watoto?
hints: Subject for they, marker for perfect, stem for read.
questions.onCorrect: The verb takes wa- when its subject is a plural of people, so watoto wamesoma means the children have read.

misconceptions.feedback: That is “they read”, with the past marker. The question asks for the perfect, -me-.
The prefix tu- means we, not they.

questions.prompt: Using the data, how do you say “we have cooked” in Swahili?
hints: Take the subject for we, the marker for the perfect and the stem for cook.
questions.onCorrect: The subject tu- appears in tulipika, the perfect marker -me- in nimesoma, and -pika in the same word as tu-, so every part is given.

misconceptions.feedback: That is “we cooked”, with the past marker -li-. The question asks for the perfect, -me-.
The prefix ni- means I. The subject for we is tu-.

questions.prompt: How do you say “you will read”?
hints: Subject for you, marker for the future, stem for read.
questions.onCorrect: The form is built from u- for you, -ta- for the future and -soma for read.

misconceptions.feedback: That is “you have read”, with the perfect marker. The future marker is -ta-.
That is “I will read”. The subject for you is u-.

questions.prompt: What is the plural of kikapu, “basket”, if kitabu goes to vitabu?
hints: Which part of kitabu changes in the plural?
questions.onCorrect: Nouns that begin with ki- take vi- in the plural, so kikapu becomes vikapu.

misconceptions.feedback: Wa- is the plural of the m- class. This noun begins with ki-.
Swahili marks the plural at the start of the noun, not at the end.

flashcards.front: What do we call a claim about what speakers ought to say, according to a rule set by an authority?
flashcards.back: A prescriptive claim ranks forms as right or wrong, while a descriptive one records what speakers do.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A prescriptive claim ranks forms as right or wrong, while a descriptive one records what speakers do.

flashcards.front: What word describes the link between the sound of a word and its meaning, set by convention and not by resemblance?
flashcards.back: The link is arbitrary, which is why different languages use unrelated sounds for the same thing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The link is arbitrary, which is why different languages use unrelated sounds for the same thing.

flashcards.front: Why can a sentence be well-formed and still make no sense?
flashcards.back: Form is about whether the words fit the patterns of the language, and sense is about whether anything could be described, so one can hold without the other.

flashcards.front: What is the term for whether the vocal folds vibrate during a sound?
flashcards.back: Voicing separates /s/ from /z/ and /p/ from /b/.

flashcards.front: Name the place of articulation of /p/, /b/ and /m/.
flashcards.back: They are made by closing both lips, so they are bilabial.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They are made by closing both lips, so they are bilabial.

flashcards.front: How many sounds are in “ship”, /ʃɪp/?
flashcards.back: The word has four letters and three sounds, because sh is one sound.

flashcards.front: What do we call two words that differ in exactly one sound and have different meanings?
flashcards.back: A minimal pair shows that the two sounds that differ are separate phonemes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A minimal pair shows that the two sounds that differ are separate phonemes.

flashcards.front: What is the plural ending sound after a voiced sound such as the /ɡ/ of “dog”?
flashcards.back: The ending takes on the voicing of the sound before it, which gives /z/.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ending takes on the voicing of the sound before it, which gives /z/.

flashcards.front: Why are aspirated and unaspirated /p/ called allophones and not separate phonemes in English?
flashcards.back: Speakers hear both as /p/ because the choice between them is set by position and never separates two English words.

flashcards.front: What is the smallest unit of form that carries meaning or grammatical function?
flashcards.back: A word may have one morpheme or several, and morphemes are counted by meaning and not by syllables.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A word may have one morpheme or several, and morphemes are counted by meaning and not by syllables.

flashcards.front: What is an affix that makes a new word, often in a new category, called: inflectional or derivational?
flashcards.back: Happy becomes happiness, so -ness is derivational, while -ed on walk gives the same verb in the past tense.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Happy becomes happiness, so -ness is derivational, while -ed on walk gives the same verb in the past tense.

flashcards.front: Why does “unbreakable” have four syllables and three morphemes?
flashcards.back: Syllables are beats of sound and morphemes are meaningful parts, and the two don't have to line up.

flashcards.front: What is a group of words that works as a single unit in a sentence called?
flashcards.back: A group is a constituent when a single word can replace it or the whole group can be moved together.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A group is a constituent when a single word can replace it or the whole group can be moved together.

flashcards.front: What is a sentence with one string of words and two structures called: structurally what?
flashcards.back: The same words can group in two ways, which gives two meanings.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same words can group in two ways, which gives two meanings.

flashcards.front: How does the substitution test show that “the small dog” is a unit but “small dog chased” is not?
flashcards.back: A single word like “it” can replace the first, and no single word can replace the second, because it cuts across two groups.

flashcards.front: What is the usual order of subject, object and verb in a plain declarative sentence called?
flashcards.back: It is the language's basic word order, which is SVO in English and SOV in Japanese.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the language's basic word order, which is SVO in English and SOV in Japanese.

flashcards.front: What is a rule called that can apply to its own output?
flashcards.back: A recursive rule lets a phrase contain a phrase of the same kind, so a sentence has no longest form.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A recursive rule lets a phrase contain a phrase of the same kind, so a sentence has no longest form.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't recursion mean every sentence has to be long?
flashcards.back: Recursion is a feature of the rule, and a speaker uses it as much as they need, so most sentences are short.

flashcards.front: If sentence A is true then B must be true. What relation does A have to B?
flashcards.back: A entails B when no situation makes A true and B false.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A entails B when no situation makes A true and B false.

flashcards.front: What is the thing in the world that a phrase picks out called: sense or reference?
flashcards.back: The morning star and the evening star have the same reference, Venus, and different senses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The morning star and the evening star have the same reference, Venus, and different senses.

flashcards.front: Why does “It is a poodle” entail “It is a dog” but not the other way?
flashcards.back: Every situation where it is a poodle is a situation where it is a dog, but a dog can be some other breed.

flashcards.front: What is something a speaker conveys beyond what the sentence entails, which can be cancelled, called?
flashcards.back: An implicature depends on the hearer assuming the speaker is cooperative.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An implicature depends on the hearer assuming the speaker is cooperative.

flashcards.front: Which of Grice's maxims asks the speaker to be relevant?
flashcards.back: The four maxims are Quantity, Quality, Relation and Manner.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The four maxims are Quantity, Quality, Relation and Manner.

flashcards.front: How does the cancel test separate an entailment from an implicature?
flashcards.back: Add a phrase that denies the consequence: a contradiction means it was entailed, and no contradiction means it was only implicated.

flashcards.front: What do we call a word in two languages that descends from one word in their common ancestor?
flashcards.back: Cognates such as Latin pater and English father are related by descent and not by borrowing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cognates such as Latin pater and English father are related by descent and not by borrowing.

flashcards.front: Latin p corresponds to which English sound, as in pater and father?
flashcards.back: The match is regular, which is why it can be used to predict forms.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The match is regular, which is why it can be used to predict forms.

flashcards.front: Why can't the similarity of pater and father be a coincidence?
flashcards.back: The same match appears in many pairs, such as pes and foot and piscis and fish, and only a shared ancestor and regular change explain it.

flashcards.front: What do we call applying a rule to a word that is an exception, as in “goed”?
flashcards.back: The error is evidence that the child has learned the rule.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The error is evidence that the child has learned the rule.

flashcards.front: What test asks a child to complete “two ___” for a made-up creature?
flashcards.back: A child who says “wugs” has not heard the word before, so must be applying a rule.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A child who says “wugs” has not heard the word before, so must be applying a rule.

flashcards.front: Explain, in your own words, why “goed” is evidence of rule learning.
flashcards.back: No adult says “goed”, so a child who says it has made the form with a rule that the child worked out for itself.

flashcards.front: What do we call a way of pronouncing a language, with the same words and grammar?
flashcards.back: An accent differs in sound only, while a dialect also has its own vocabulary and grammar.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An accent differs in sound only, while a dialect also has its own vocabulary and grammar.

flashcards.front: In Labov's study, which store had the highest share of employees pronouncing the r?
flashcards.back: The share was highest in the highest-ranked store and lowest in the lowest-ranked one.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The share was highest in the highest-ranked store and lowest in the lowest-ranked one.

flashcards.front: Why isn't a standard variety better in itself than a non-standard one?
flashcards.back: It is favoured because of the status of the people who use it, and linguistically every variety works equally well for its speakers.

flashcards.front: What is a table of the forms of a word, or of a set of words, called?
flashcards.back: A paradigm sets forms side by side so you can see which part changes with what.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A paradigm sets forms side by side so you can see which part changes with what.

flashcards.front: In Swahili, which prefix means “they” in walisoma?
flashcards.back: The prefix wa- is the subject for they and also the plural of nouns like mtoto.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The prefix wa- is the subject for they and also the plural of nouns like mtoto.

flashcards.front: Why is it better to compare the parts of the forms than to read the translations alone?
flashcards.back: The translations say what a form means, but only lining up the forms shows which part carries which meaning, so a new form can be built.
